SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

noisy adjective

also rowdy

classical

Mart. 5.84.2: clāmōsō … ā magistrō
Quint. 6.4.15: turbidus et clāmōsus altercātor (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. noisy

clāmōsus, clāmōsa, clāmōsum

adjective

noisy, always shouting; full of noise

Of people who shout, and of places full of shouting. Mostly post-Augustan (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • jam trīstis nucibus puer relictīs clāmōsō revocātur ā magistrō

    now the sad boy leaves his nuts and is called back by the shouting schoolmasterMart. 5.84.1–2

  • vōx ista quā strepunt avēs stantēs sub ipsō culmine

    that chatter the birds make, perched under the ridge of the roofPrud. Cath. 1.13–14

  • Quid strepitis, puerī? Īnfāns dormit.

    Why are you so noisy, children? The baby is asleep.composed

Other words

  • tumultuōsus, tumultuōsa, tumultuōsum — full of din and bustle

    adjective · also used · classical · Plaut. Trin. 5.2.52: tam tumultuōsō sonitū (Lewis & Short)

  • strepō, strepere, strepuī — make a noise, clatter, chatter

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Prud. Cath. 1.13: vōx ista quā strepunt avēs; M-O s.v. noisy: strepēns

    Latin often says “noisy” with this verb.

See also quiet!, be quiet.

SourcesLewis & Short: clamosus · Lewis & Short: tumultuosus · Lewis & Short: strepo

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. noisy.

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-martialis, loci-prudentius), checked against the editions named there.
